summary: Describes service classes configured with Differentiated Services and recommends how to use and build them using DSCPs, traffic conditioners, per-hop behaviors and active queue management. It states that no particular DSCP use is strictly required. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Differentiated Services lets a network treat packets in many different ways, but it does not say which combination to use. This memo gives ready-made settings for twelve common kinds of traffic, so an administrator can start from a known plan. Only the plain best-effort class is required; the rest are optional.

subtitle: An Informational guide that turns the DiffServ toolkit into ready-made settings for twelve kinds of network traffic.

tldr.problem: Differentiated Services gives a network powerful but general tools for treating packets differently, and it is hard for a non-expert to choose settings; networks that mark and treat traffic inconsistently lose quality of service from end to end.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines twelve service classes (two for network control, ten for user traffic) and recommends a DSCP, an edge conditioner, a PHB, a queuing style and an AQM setting for each.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, not a standard; it says no particular DSCP, PHB or AQM is strictly required, and it has been updated by RFC 5865 and RFC 8622.

today: RFC 4594 is an Informational memo and has not been obsoleted. It is listed as updated by RFC 5865 and RFC 8622. The RFC itself says it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: Why Service Classes Are Needed
sections.content:
The RFC explains its purpose with an analogy: the Differentiated Services specifications are a toolkit of powerful tools, but a non-expert who only wants to build one thing can find the toolkit hard to use. This memo is a set of project plans that show how to assemble the pieces for common kinds of traffic.

A service class is a set of traffic that needs particular delay, loss and delay-variation (jitter) behavior from the network. Classes group applications with similar needs, so a new application can be placed in an existing class. The RFC defines twelve classes: two for network operation and ten for user traffic, and it expects administrators to implement only the subset they need.

The RFC states plainly that nothing requires a particular DSCP, traffic conditioner, per-hop behavior (PHB) or Active Queue Management (AQM) mechanism for a given class, but that applying them consistently helps policy and interoperability. Only the Default Forwarding Standard class is REQUIRED; all other classes are OPTIONAL.
sections.plainLanguage: Differentiated Services lets a network treat packets in many different ways, but it does not say which combination to use. This memo gives ready-made settings for twelve common kinds of traffic, so an administrator can start from a known plan. Only one setting, the plain best-effort class, is required; the rest are optional.

sections.title: The Building Blocks: Queues, AQM, Conditioners and PHBs
sections.content:
This section recaps the pieces the classes are built from. A priority queue empties the highest-priority queue first; it lowers delay and variation in delay but must not starve lower queues. A rate queue, such as Weighted Fair Queuing (WFQ) or Weighted Round Robin (WRR), empties each queue at a set rate.

Active Queue Management (AQM) drops or marks packets to control how deep a queue grows. The best-known example is Random Early Detection (RED), which sets a minimum and a maximum threshold on the average queue depth. A traffic conditioner measures arriving traffic at the first router and drops, marks or shapes it, usually with token bucket meters: one bucket for CS and EF, and usually two for AF.

A DSCP is a number from 0 to 63 placed in an IP packet to mark which class it belongs to; half the values are reserved for standardized services and half are for local use. A PHB, or per-hop behavior, is the treatment a class receives at each router. Four basic behaviors are used: Default Forwarding (DF), Assured Forwarding (AF), Expedited Forwarding (EF) and Class Selector (CS).
sections.plainLanguage: Routers sort traffic by putting packets into separate waiting lines and choosing which line to empty first. Some lines are emptied by priority, and others at a fixed rate. Each packet carries a number that says which line it belongs in, and those markings are what the classes use.

sections.title: The Twelve Service Classes and Their Markings
sections.content:
Traffic is divided into network control and user traffic. Network control has Network Control for routing and OAM for operations, administration and management. User traffic has ten classes: Telephony, Signaling, Multimedia Conferencing, Real-Time Interactive, Multimedia Streaming, Broadcast Video, Low-Latency Data, High-Throughput Data, Standard and Low-Priority Data.

The user classes are grouped into four application categories: application control, media-oriented, data and best effort. Each is tagged with a flow behavior (elastic, rate adaptive or inelastic) and an end-user rating from ITU-T G.1010 (interactive, responsive, timely or non-critical).

Figure 3 lists the recommended DSCP for each class, and the RFC says it is RECOMMENDED that this mapping be preserved end to end. The names and their order imply no priority; they are reference names only, and administrators may choose different names. A packet marked with a DSCP the network does not support SHOULD be forwarded using the Standard class.
sections.plainLanguage: The traffic is sorted into twelve groups: two that keep the network running and ten for user applications such as voice calls, video and file transfer. Each group is given its own packet marking, and the memo recommends that every network use the same marking for the same group, so the treatment stays consistent from end to end.

sections.title: How Each Class Is Configured
sections.content:
Sections 3 and 4 give a recipe for each class. Network Control (CS6) carries routing traffic such as OSPF, BGP, ISIS and RIP, uses rate queuing with AQM, and must not be used by user traffic. Telephony (EF) uses the EF PHB of RFC 3246 with a priority queue, because voice packets are inelastic and do not react to loss or delay; AQM SHOULD NOT be applied to EF traffic.

Signaling (CS5), Real-Time Interactive (CS4) and Broadcast Video (CS3) use Class Selector PHBs with rate queuing and single-rate policers, and no AQM. The AF-based classes, namely Multimedia Conferencing (AF4x), Multimedia Streaming (AF3x), Low-Latency Data (AF2x) and High-Throughput Data (AF1x), use the AF PHB of RFC 2597 with a three-color marker and AQM per DSCP.

Standard uses Default Forwarding (DF) with AQM, and Low-Priority Data uses CS1 with the lower-effort PHB of RFC 3662. Edge conditioners police untrusted sources, and traffic marked with an unsupported DSCP is treated as Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Each group gets its own rules. Voice calls get a separate fast line, ordinary web traffic gets the default treatment, and background transfers are allowed to wait. At the edge of the network, routers check that incoming packets are marked as the sender is entitled to, and drop or re-mark the rest.

sections.title: Three Deployment Examples
sections.content:
The RFC expects administrators to start with three or four user classes and add more as needed. Example 1 is a provider offering reliable VoIP, a low-delay assured-bandwidth data service and normal Internet service; it uses six classes: Network Control, Standard, Telephony, Signaling, Low-Latency Data and OAM.

Example 2 grows that network by four classes (Real-Time Interactive, Broadcast Video, Multimedia Streaming and High-Throughput Data) to add desktop video conferencing, IPTV and on-demand movies, and network storage and backup, giving ten classes in all. Example 3 is an enterprise network that needs nine classes. In every example, a packet with an unsupported DSCP SHOULD be forwarded as Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: A network can begin with a few groups and add more as its services grow. The memo shows three examples: a small provider setup, a larger provider setup with video, and an enterprise network. Each larger example keeps the earlier groups and simply adds new ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says that if the policy it describes is implemented as written, the network does nothing it had not already allowed, so no new security issues should arise. A policy can still be applied incorrectly, and the network SHOULD detect and deal with that.

The known flaw is that bandwidth reserved for one service, such as voice, can be used by another service or by attack traffic. This is built into DiffServ, which trusts packet markings. Where reservation or priority queuing is used, authentication and flow admission are recommended. Some classes, such as Network Control, are not open to users at all, and such traffic should be dropped or remarked by ingress filters.

Where a class is available under an SLA only to authenticated users, authentication and authorization services are required.
sections.plainLanguage: A network that trusts packet markings can be abused by anyone who marks ordinary traffic as high priority. When a service reserves bandwidth, the memo recommends checking that only authorised traffic uses it. Access to some classes is blocked altogether at the edge of the network.

viz.caption: SIX MECHANISMS THE SERVICE CLASSES ARE BUILT FROM

items.title: Priority queuing
items.text: Empties the highest-priority queue first; lowers delay and jitter but must not starve lower queues.

items.title: Rate queuing
items.text: Weighted Fair Queuing or Weighted Round Robin empties each queue at a set rate.

items.title: Active Queue Management
items.text: Drops or marks packets to control queue depth; the classic example is RED.

items.title: Traffic conditioning
items.text: Measures traffic at the first router and drops, marks or shapes it.

items.title: DSCP
items.text: A number from 0 to 63 in each packet that says which class it belongs to.

items.title: Per-hop behavior
items.text: The treatment a class receives at each router, such as DF, AF, EF or CS.

viz.caption: RECOMMENDED SERVICE CLASS TO DSCP MAPPING (FIGURE 3)

items.label: Real-Time Interactive
items.desc: DSCP 100000. Video conferencing and interactive gaming.

items.label: Multimedia Streaming
items.desc: 011010, 011100, 011110. Streaming video and audio on demand.

items.label: Broadcast Video
items.desc: DSCP 011000. Broadcast TV and live events.

items.label: Low-Priority Data
items.desc: DSCP 001000. Flows with no bandwidth assurance.
